questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Identify what makes a delegate's mandate fixed-term
questions.stem: Your consortium's charter renews technical delegate seats every six years by a recorded vote. Which feature makes the mandate fixed-term?

options.text: The charter names a set period for the mandate and requires a recorded vote to renew it.
Delegates may be dismissed by the secretariat director whenever the work programme changes.
options.misconception: treats the secretariat as the source of delegate authority

options.text: Delegates keep their seat indefinitely once the assembly has confirmed the appointment.
options.misconception: assumes assembly appointment grants tenure for life

options.text: The mandate lasts until the delegate's employer withdraws the nomination, with no fixed end.
options.misconception: believes the home organisation controls the end of tenure

questions.explanation: A fixed term sets an end date and requires renewal by the assembly, so authority is re-granted periodically. The distractors describe dismissal at will, permanent tenure, or control by the employer.
questions.hint: Ask what formally ends the mandate without removing the person.

options.misconception: counts political commitments as legally binding

options.text: Twelve, because treaties are the only instruments here that create binding obligations.
Seventeen, because memoranda of understanding become binding once signed.
options.misconception: assumes signature alone makes a memorandum binding

options.text: Twenty, because every instrument in the archive is enforceable as written.
options.misconception: treats all archived instruments as legally enforceable

questions.explanation: Only the twelve treaties in the table carry binding legal obligations; commitments and memoranda are political. Adding non-binding instruments to treaties, or treating signature as binding, overstates the count.
questions.hint: Count only the row that creates enforceable obligations.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Explain how an unelected body can be held accountable
questions.stem: A regional standards board is staffed by technical experts appointed by member governments rather than elected by citizens. Explain how such a body can still be held accountable.

answer.exemplar: An appointed board can be accountable through reporting duties, published minutes, judicial or audit review of its decisions, fixed mandates, and an appeals route open to affected parties. Accountability here does not require elections; it requires that reasons be disclosed, outputs be reviewable by outsiders, and members can be challenged or replaced when performance falls short.

questions.explanation: Accountability comes from external review, disclosure, and the possibility of challenge rather than from election alone. Without those features, appointment by governments leaves the board answerable only to the officials who created it.
questions.hint: Accountability can rest on review and disclosure, not votes.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: Characteristics of a global public good
questions.learningObjective: Apply the non-excludability test to a described arrangement

stimulus.body: A transboundary water-sharing arrangement obliges every basin state to keep abstraction within an agreed cap, regardless of whether any other state contributes. The draft note explains that the arrangement protects a shared aquifer that no single state owns and that every user benefits from its protection, whether or not they paid for it.

questions.stem: Using only the draft note above, which feature of the arrangement indicates that the resource it protects is close to a global public good?

options.text: The cap is written into a binding legal instrument that states must accept.
options.misconception: treats legal binding as the defining property of a public good

options.text: Every basin state that benefits must also pay an equal share of the cost.
options.misconception: assumes public goods must be paid for by every user

options.text: Users benefit from the protected aquifer whether or not they contributed to the arrangement.
No state can withdraw from the arrangement once it has entered into force.
options.misconception: confuses irreversibility of commitment with non-excludability

questions.explanation: Non-excludability means benefits cannot be withheld from non-contributors, which the note describes directly. Legal binding concerns commitment, and cost-sharing concerns financing; neither defines the good itself.
questions.hint: Focus on whether a non-contributor still receives the benefit.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Identify free-riding in a shared-cost arrangement

stimulus.body: Eleven firms share the cost of a common geotechnical survey, and each firm benefits from its results. The agreement divides the bill equally, and firms that pay their share may report their contributions publicly. One firm has begun paying nothing while continuing to use the survey data.

questions.stem: Given the arrangement described above, what behaviour does the firm that pays nothing represent, and what does it do to the other firms?

options.text: It represents shirking on a public task, since no one is assigned the survey work.
options.misconception: confuses non-payment with refusal of assigned duties

options.text: It represents a legitimate discount for firms that contribute their own data instead.
options.misconception: invents an off-book contribution the arrangement lacks

options.text: It represents a dispute over the quality of the survey method between members.
options.misconception: recasts a payment failure as a technical disagreement

options.text: It represents free-riding: it takes the shared benefit while shifting cost onto the others.

questions.explanation: The firm uses the survey without paying, which is free-riding on a shared, non-excludable good. Shifting its share onto the ten paying firms raises their cost and can push some of them out of the arrangement.
questions.hint: One member benefits and avoids cost: name that pattern.

questions.learningObjective: Sequence the stages from proposal to binding commitment
questions.stem: A new load standard moves through a technical committee, a plenum of member states, and a deposit with the registrar. Which ordering best reflects how a proposal becomes a binding commitment?

options.text: Committee draft, adoption by the assembly, entry into force once the required ratifications are deposited.
Entry into force on deposit of the first instrument, committee drafting, and later adoption by the assembly.
options.misconception: reverses the order so entry into force precedes drafting

options.text: Committee drafting, deposit by individual states, and formal adoption by the assembly after the last ratification.
options.misconception: puts deposit before adoption, inverting the real sequence

options.text: Assembly adoption, entry into force, and committee drafting that merely tidies the finished text.
options.misconception: makes drafting a formality that follows adoption

questions.explanation: A proposal is drafted technically, adopted by the assembly, and only becomes binding when enough ratifications are deposited. Reversing any of these steps misstates when obligations actually start.
questions.hint: Drafting comes first, then adoption, then force.

questions.topic: Why states comply with rules they did not write
questions.learningObjective: Combine a condition and a conclusion about compliance
questions.stem: A state signed a technical standard years ago but helped write only part of it. If the standard has become the basis for market access that the state values, which inference about compliance is best supported, and why?

options.text: The state will comply because it is legally obliged, since signature alone created the duty.
options.misconception: treats signature as the sole source of legal obligation

options.text: The state will not comply because it never drafted the technical provisions.
options.misconception: assumes only authors of a rule accept its authority

options.text: Compliance is likely because the rule now serves the state's own interests.
Compliance is likely because the secretariat can impose penalties without a legal process.
options.misconception: assumes a secretariat can punish states unilaterally

questions.explanation: Compliance is strongest where a rule aligns with a state's interests or is needed for market access it values. Signature creates a duty only if the instrument requires ratification, and authorship is not what gives a rule force.
questions.hint: Ask why the rule is useful to the state itself.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Distinguish self-limitation of sovereignty from its elimination
questions.stem: A state ratifies a maritime safety convention that sets minimum standards for its vessels. Which statement best describes the effect of ratification on that state's sovereignty?

options.text: Sovereignty is transferred to the convention's secretariat, which now issues the state's shipping rules.
options.misconception: believes ratification transfers sovereignty to the secretariat

options.text: Sovereignty is suspended until the state withdraws, because the convention overrides domestic law.
options.misconception: confuses binding rules with the total loss of sovereign power

options.text: Sovereignty is unchanged because only domestic legislatures can create obligations that bind states.
options.misconception: denies that international obligations can bind at all

options.text: Sovereignty is retained but limited, because the state accepted obligations it may not violate freely.

questions.explanation: A state binds itself by consent, so sovereignty continues but is exercised within agreed limits. Ratification neither transfers authority to a secretariat nor removes the state's capacity to govern.
questions.hint: Consent limits how a state may act without removing it.

questions.learningObjective: Interpret membership data for an expert community
questions.stem: An expert panel on structural safety has 60 members: 45 from national standards bodies, 10 from universities, and 5 from contractors. How many members are outside the bodies that will apply the panel's guidance?

options.text: Fifteen, counting the university and contractor members together.
Five, because only the contractor members sit outside the applying bodies.
options.misconception: counts only contractors and ignores university members

options.text: Ten, because university members work for the standards bodies by affiliation.
options.misconception: assumes university members are affiliated to standards bodies

options.text: Forty-five, because the panel's guidance binds mainly the standards bodies themselves.
options.misconception: counts the applying bodies as the outsiders

questions.explanation: Universities and contractors together make 10 plus 5, which is 15 members outside the standards bodies. Only those bodies will apply the guidance directly, so the remaining 45 are the audience for implementation.
questions.hint: Add the two groups that are not standards bodies.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Explain why fixed-term delegacy supports accountability
questions.stem: A standards forum appoints member-state delegates to six-year terms that can be renewed by the assembly. Explain how fixed-term delegacy affects the accountability of those delegates.

answer.exemplar: A fixed term makes the mandate conditional on periodic review, so delegates must expect to justify their conduct to the assembly that can renew or replace them. Because the term ends even without misconduct, officeholders have an incentive to seek continued support rather than to hide behind assumed permanence, and the assembly gains a regular point at which performance, conflicts of interest, and attendance can be examined.

questions.explanation: Fixed terms give the appointing body a scheduled occasion to renew, amend, or withdraw authority. That converts a delegate into a periodically reviewable officeholder instead of a permanent insider of the forum.
questions.hint: Think about the scheduled point of review.

questions.hint: Divide the binding count by the total, then multiply by 100.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Identify accountability mechanisms in a described arrangement

stimulus.body: The aviation safety commission publishes the minutes of every panel decision, submits its annual work programme to the transport committee for approval, and may be required to answer written questions from the legislature. Individual staff members are named in the minutes with the vote they cast on each finding.

questions.stem: Based on the excerpt above, which combination most clearly makes the commission accountable despite having no elected members?

options.text: Publication of minutes and legislative questioning, but not approval of its work programme.
options.misconception: misses legislative approval of the work programme as a control

options.text: Publication of minutes, parliamentary questioning, and legislative approval of its work programme.
Named votes on individual findings, but not publication of the meeting minutes.
options.misconception: omits the minutes, which are the main disclosure tool

options.text: Only the publication of minutes, since the other measures touch the committee not the commission.
options.misconception: believes only external disclosure counts as accountability

questions.explanation: Accountability here comes from combining disclosure with review: published minutes, questions answered by the legislature, and approval of the work programme. Naming individuals adds transparency, but on its own it does not let anyone challenge the body's work.
questions.hint: Look for both disclosure and someone able to check it.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: A two-thirds threshold in a large assembly
questions.learningObjective: Evaluate whether a vote cleared a supermajority threshold

stimulus.body: The assembly of a 96-seat regional council can adopt binding technical rules only by a two-thirds vote of all seats. A recent session had 88 members present and the chair confirmed that a full quorum was required before voting began.

questions.stem: In the session described above, the council voted 59 in favour and 27 against, with 2 abstentions among the 88 members present. Did the vote clear the two-thirds threshold?

options.text: Yes, because 59 out of 88 present exceeds two thirds of those voting.
options.misconception: measures the threshold against votes cast rather than all seats

options.text: No, because a two-thirds majority needs at least 65 votes in favour.
options.misconception: applies the rule to those present and ignores abstentions

options.text: No, because two thirds of all 96 seats is 64, and only 59 were in favour.
Yes, because abstentions are excluded, leaving 86 votes of which 59 is a clear majority.
options.misconception: assumes a supermajority needs only a simple majority

questions.explanation: Two thirds of all 96 seats is 64 votes, and the chair required a quorum of all seats, so 59 is short. Measuring against those present or those voting would wrongly relax the rule.
questions.hint: Multiply the threshold by the full membership, not the votes cast.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: Characteristics of a global public good
questions.learningObjective: Identify a global public good from its defining properties
questions.stem: A measure that stops the release of a disease-resistant seed variety spreads to all countries at once, and every country benefits from that spread whether or not it funded the research. Which best captures the relevant property?

options.text: The benefits are non-rival and cannot be withheld from countries that did not contribute.
The research was funded by many countries, so the measure must be a global public good.
options.misconception: infers public-good status from how many countries funded it

options.text: The measure is a global public good because it is negotiated and signed by many states.
options.misconception: confuses a widely negotiated treaty with a public good

options.text: The measure is a global public good only if a treaty is negotiated before the release happens.
options.misconception: assumes a legal instrument is a precondition for a public good

questions.explanation: A public good is non-rival and non-excludable: one country's use does not reduce another's benefit and non-contributors are not cut off. Financing arrangements and treaty signature describe how the measure was made, not what makes it a public good.
questions.hint: Ask what happens if a non-contributor tries to benefit.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Combine a free-rider's payoff with its effect on the group
questions.stem: Ten firms share a survey costing 400,000 equally, so each share is 40,000. One firm pays nothing and uses the results. If its share is redistributed, what is the extra cost borne by each of the nine paying firms?

options.text: 4,000, since 40,000 is spread across nine firms rather than ten.
options.misconception: divides the free rider's share by nine and calls it extra cost

options.text: 40,000, because the whole share is added to each paying firm's own bill.
options.misconception: adds the full share to every firm instead of splitting it

options.text: 10,000, because the non-paying firm's advantage is spread over the whole group.
options.misconception: spreads the cost over ten firms including the free rider

options.text: 4,444, because 40,000 divided by nine paying firms is the added burden each carries.

questions.explanation: 40,000 spread over nine paying firms is about 4,444 each, which is the added burden that creates the incentive to free-ride. Dividing by ten ignores the free rider, and charging the full share to each firm overstates the effect.
questions.hint: Divide the unpaid share by the number of firms still paying.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Distinguish signature from entry into force
questions.stem: A coastal state has signed a protocol but not yet deposited its instrument of ratification, and 30 of 60 parties have deposited theirs. What is the protocol's legal status for that state?

options.text: Fully binding, because signature alone creates the full legal effect of the protocol.
options.misconception: treats signature as equivalent to ratification

options.text: Not yet binding on that state, because the protocol requires ratification before entry into force.
Binding, because the majority of parties have ratified and the state may not opt out.
options.misconception: believes majority ratification binds a non-ratifying state

options.text: Partially binding, since the state must respect the protocol's aims while it decides.
options.misconception: invents an obligation to respect aims before ratification

questions.explanation: Under the common design, a protocol binds the states that ratify it and enters into force among them once the threshold is met. Signature alone carries no such duty, and the majority's ratification cannot impose it on a non-ratifying state.
questions.hint: Check what the instrument requires before obligations attach.

options.misconception: treats partial compliance as if it were non-compliance

100, because every audited jurisdiction had at least begun work on the standard.
options.misconception: assumes starting work equals reaching compliance

options.misconception: halves partial compliance, which the audit did not do

questions.explanation: 31 plus 5 is 36 of 40 jurisdictions, which is 90 percent at least partly compliant. Halving partial compliance or excluding it entirely produces figures the audit does not support.
questions.hint: Add full and partial, then divide by the audited total.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Explain the effect of a treaty on state sovereignty
questions.stem: A state has ratified a fisheries protocol that limits how much it may catch in a shared sea. Explain what the protocol does and does not do to that state's sovereignty.

answer.exemplar: The protocol narrows the range of lawful action but leaves the state sovereign, because the state itself consented to the limit and can amend, suspend, or withdraw according to the treaty's own terms. It does not hand authority to the depositary or any other state, nor does it remove the state's ability to act in every other domain. Sovereignty persists as the state's capacity to govern; what changes is the self-imposed restraint it accepts while the obligations remain in force.

questions.explanation: A treaty limits how a state may act but does not transfer or erase sovereignty, since the state consented and retains its powers elsewhere. Withdrawal is possible but usually governed by the treaty's own terms.
questions.hint: Separate restraint of action from loss of authority.

questions.learningObjective: Derive a delegate's maximum tenure from a quoted rule

stimulus.body: Article 6 of the forum's rules states that the term of office of a member delegation is three years. options.misconception: misses the one further term allowed by the quoted article

options.text: Six years, because a delegation is appointed once and then continues until replaced.
options.misconception: treats replacement as the only route out of the mandate

options.text: Unlimited, because a delegation may serve as an observer for any part of its term.
options.misconception: mistakes an observer capacity for an open-ended tenure

options.text: Six years, three years plus one further three-year term, if the assembly reappoints it.

questions.explanation: The rules allow an initial three-year term and one further three-year term by assembly decision, so six years is the maximum. Early replacement shortens the mandate but does not extend it, and observer status adds no time.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Compute the burden of free-riding on paying members
questions.stem: Eight engineering firms share a cost of 240,000 equally, but two firms pay nothing and use the results. How much extra does each of the six paying firms now carry?

options.text: 7,500, because the 60,000 unpaid share is spread over all eight firms.
options.misconception: spreads the unpaid share over firms that also free-ride

options.text: 10,000, because the 60,000 unpaid share is spread over the six paying firms.
26,667, because two thirds of the total cost now falls on the remaining six firms.
options.misconception: applies a two-thirds ratio the arithmetic does not support

options.text: 30,000, because the paying firms must cover each free rider's whole original share.
options.misconception: adds the full unpaid share to each paying firm's bill

questions.explanation: Each firm's equal share is 240,000 divided by 8, which is 30,000, so the two free riders leave 60,000 for six paying firms, which is 10,000 each. Spreading it over eight firms, or adding the whole share to each bill, misstates the allocation.
questions.hint: Find the unpaid share, then divide it by the paying firms.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Explain the steps that convert a proposal into a binding commitment
questions.stem: A technical committee has drafted a standard on fatigue loading, the assembly has adopted it, and only some states have deposited ratifications. Explain the path from draft to binding commitment and where it currently stands.

answer.exemplar: The draft has three distinct stages to pass through. The technical committee prepares and validates the text, the assembly adopts it, and the deposit of instruments of ratification by the required number of parties triggers entry into force for those parties. Only the states that have deposited are bound, and a state that has only signed remains free of the obligation unless the text says otherwise. Because the count of ratifications has not reached the threshold, the standard is not yet in force even though it has already been adopted.

questions.explanation: Drafting establishes technical content, adoption gives the text political authority, and ratification triggers legal force for those who ratify. Without the threshold met, the standard is adopted but not yet in force.
questions.hint: Separate adoption from the step that creates legal force.

questions.hint: Weight each jurisdiction, divide by the number, then scale.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Read a withdrawal clause and state its effect on obligations

stimulus.body: The withdrawal clause of the maritime convention provides that a party may withdraw at any time after three years from the date the convention entered into force for that party, on written notice to the depositary. The convention also provides that obligations concerning the safety of vessels in shared waters survive the withdrawal of the party for a period of five years from the effective date of its withdrawal.

questions.stem: According to the quoted clause, what follows for a state that withdraws from the convention?

options.text: It must observe the shared-water safety obligations for five years after its withdrawal takes effect.
It is free of all obligations immediately, because withdrawal is available at any time without notice.
options.misconception: misses the notice requirement and the surviving safety duties

options.text: It must wait three years after entry into force before it may give notice, and then it is free.
options.misconception: treats the surviving safety duties as ending with withdrawal

options.text: It may withdraw only with the consent of every other party, since safety duties are collective.
options.misconception: assumes withdrawal requires unanimous consent of other parties

questions.explanation: The clause explicitly preserves the shared-water safety obligations for five years after withdrawal takes effect. The three-year rule only governs when notice may be given, and withdrawal is unilateral once that condition is met.
questions.hint: Look for the obligations that explicitly survive withdrawal.

options.text: It publishes regularly, and regular publication is the defining feature of the group.
options.misconception: reduces community status to the frequency of publication

options.text: It includes suppliers, and an interest in selling equipment gives members a shared view.
options.misconception: assumes commercial interest produces shared expertise

options.text: It meets four times a year, and regular meetings define the community more than membership does.
options.misconception: treats meeting frequency as the defining criterion

options.text: It shares a common technical domain in which members hold and exchange expert knowledge.

questions.explanation: An epistemic community is defined by a shared domain of expertise and the exchange of knowledge within it, which this group demonstrates. Publication frequency, meeting rhythm, and commercial interests describe the group's activity, not the source of its community.

options.misconception: praises permanence, which weakens renewal-based scrutiny

options.text: A larger committee and a rule that the chair alone may approve minutes.
options.misconception: misses that unchecked chair power weakens accountability

options.text: Published committee minutes, a published conflict-of-interest register, and a renewable term.
An expanded secretariat mandate and faster voting procedures inside committees.
options.misconception: confuses administrative speed with a check on members' conduct

questions.explanation: Accountability comes from disclosure of how a decision was reached, disclosure of interests, and a point at which authority can be renewed or withdrawn. Faster procedures and larger bodies change how much work happens but add no scrutiny of members.

The claim succeeds, because adoption by the assembly converts any statement into a legal obligation.
options.misconception: assumes adoption alone converts any text into binding law

options.text: The claim fails, because only treaties ratified by states can create obligations between members.

options.text: The legislature can overturn a tariff decision, giving it a real prospect of being overruled.

options.misconception: treats publication alone as the decisive constraint

options.text: The regulator's staff are appointed for fixed terms, which keeps its work stable.
options.misconception: mistakes tenure stability for a check on decisions

Yes, because 72 out of the 102 votes cast is more than two thirds.
options.misconception: measures the threshold against votes cast rather than all seats

options.text: No, because the 18 abstentions count as votes against the standard.
options.misconception: counts abstentions as opposition without any rule to that effect

options.text: Yes, because abstentions are excluded and 72 beats two thirds of 102.
options.misconception: repeats the votes-cast error and adds an unjustified exclusion

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Explain why a shared good is vulnerable to free-riding
questions.stem: A consortium funds a common safety standard that every member benefits from, but the benefit does not depend on whether a particular member pays. Explain why this arrangement invites free-riding and what follows for the consortium's funding.

answer.exemplar: Because the benefit is non-excludable, a member can keep the full value of the safety standard while avoiding its cost, so paying is not individually necessary to secure the benefit. Rational members who can be sure their own contribution will not change the outcome have an incentive to under-contribute, and if enough act on it the standard is underfunded or abandoned. Common fixes are compulsory shares, public reporting of each member's contribution, and benefits that can be withheld from non-contributors, each of which changes the incentive rather than asking members to be voluntarily generous.

questions.explanation: When benefits cannot be excluded, individual firms gain from the shared good even if they contribute nothing, so voluntary contributions tend to fall short of what the good requires. The fix is to change the incentive, not to appeal to fairness.
questions.hint: Ask what each member gains by paying nothing.

options.text: On 1 March, because the entry-into-force trigger is the deposit of the sixtieth instrument.
options.misconception: ignores the thirty-day period that follows the trigger

options.text: On 30 March, because the thirty days must be counted back from the deposit date.
options.misconception: counts the thirty days backwards instead of forwards

options.text: On 30 March, because the deposit day itself counts as the first of the thirty days.
options.misconception: counts the deposit date as day one of the thirty

options.text: On 31 March, being the thirtieth day after the deposit of the sixtieth instrument.

questions.explanation: The clause sets the trigger at the sixtieth deposit and requires thirty days to run from it, so the thirtieth day after 1 March is 31 March. Counting backwards or including the deposit day misreads the clause.
questions.hint: Add thirty days to the trigger date, excluding the deposit day.

options.misconception: relies on an insurance consequence the scenario never mentions

options.text: The claim is too weak, because states may withdraw at any moment without consequence.
options.misconception: assumes withdrawal is costless and free of conditions

The claim is wrong, because treaties only ever constrain private firms rather than states.
options.misconception: denies that treaties bind states at all

options.misconception: ignores the partial delivery of the remaining experts

options.text: 63, because the three experts remaining each owe their full quota of 18 plus 9.
options.misconception: adds a quota to the expert count and misreads the shortfall

options.misconception: reads the target as if all but the last items were complete

options.text: 54, because the three unfinished experts still owe 18 items each.

options.misconception: treats not-yet-in-force treaties as non-binding

options.misconception: assumes entry into force is required before a treaty binds

90, because every instrument except the 30 non-binding ones creates binding obligations.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Explain how oversight holds an appointed body accountable
questions.stem: A regional water regulator has no elected members, but its decisions are published, its annual budget is approved by a legislature, and any affected party may petition the appeals panel. Explain how these features make it accountable.

answer.exemplar: Accountability here comes from four separate channels rather than from election. Publication makes the reasoning behind each decision visible and comparable over time; legislative approval of the budget gives an elected body leverage over what the regulator does and what it spends; the petitions route lets affected parties challenge individual decisions on stated grounds; and the appeals panel supplies a forum in which a decision can actually be overturned. Together these make the regulator answerable to others, which is what accountability means, even though nobody in it was chosen by voters.

questions.explanation: Accountability needs reasons that outsiders can see, a body that can reverse or constrain the regulator, and a route for affected parties to challenge it. Elections are one way to achieve this, not the only one.
questions.hint: Name who can see the work, who can constrain it, and who can challenge it.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Compare fixed-term and open-ended delegation
questions.stem: One standards forum uses five-year renewable terms for delegates and another grants seats until the forum's own dissolution. Explain the main accountability difference between the two arrangements.

answer.exemplar: In the first arrangement the delegate's authority expires on a fixed date and can be renewed, so the appointing assembly retains a recurring chance to review performance, replace individuals, and adjust the delegation's composition. The second arrangement removes that recurring checkpoint: once admitted, a delegate serves until the forum itself ends, which lengthens the horizon over which habits of influence and private interests can accumulate. The difference is not about competence or trust but about whether the appointing body retains a usable, periodic occasion to say yes again.

questions.explanation: A renewable term gives the appointing body a standing opportunity to review or replace the delegate, while an open-ended seat removes that checkpoint. The difference shows up in periodic review, not in the delegate's expertise.

questions.topic: A binding instrument and a non-binding one
questions.learningObjective: Compute the binding share of a set of instruments
questions.stem: An assembly votes on 24 instruments and 18 of them reach the binding threshold while the remaining 6 are adopted only as political statements. What percentage of the instruments voted on are binding?
questions.explanation: 18 out of 24 is 0.75, so 75 percent of the instruments are binding. Counting the political statements as binding, or measuring the share only among those that passed, would distort the figure.
questions.hint: Divide the binding count by the total voted, then scale by 100.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Derive oversight mechanisms from a quoted charter

stimulus.body: The oversight charter states that the secretariat's director is appointed by the assembly for a term of four years, may be reappointed once, and is removable by a two-thirds vote of the assembly. The charter also requires that the director's budget be approved annually by the assembly, and that an annual report of the secretariat's decisions be published in full.

questions.stem: Based on the quoted charter, which statement about the secretariat director's accountability is correct?

options.text: The director is effectively unaccountable, because the assembly has no mechanism to remove him.
options.misconception: ignores the removal vote stated in the charter

options.text: The director is accountable only for spending, since the budget is the only assembly power listed.
options.misconception: treats budget approval as the sole oversight mechanism

options.text: The director faces several controls: a renewable term, a removal vote, budget approval, and published reporting.
The director is unconstrained, because a four-year term guarantees he acts independently.
options.misconception: mistakes a fixed term for freedom from oversight

questions.explanation: The charter lists four distinct controls on the director, so accountability does not rest on the single budget power. A renewable term is not immunity, since reappointment and a removal vote both sit with the assembly.
questions.hint: Count the separate powers the assembly retains.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: A two-thirds threshold in a large assembly
questions.learningObjective: Assess a proposed reinterpretation of a voting rule

stimulus.body: A 210-seat council has adopted a standing rule that binding technical standards require a two-thirds vote of the membership, and the secretariat has always applied the rule to the full 210 seats. Two members have asked the chair to reinterpret the rule as applying only to those voting, arguing that the current reading is impractical for large assemblies.

questions.stem: In the scenario above, how should the secretariat treat the request to reinterpret the voting threshold?

options.text: Reject it, because the standing rule is applied to membership and a reinterpretation would need the assembly.
Accept it, because a practical difficulty in large assemblies justifies a flexible reading.
options.misconception: lets convenience override the standing rule

options.text: Accept it, because the chair has the power to interpret the assembly's rules of procedure.
options.misconception: assumes the chair may unilaterally interpret binding rules

options.text: Refer it to the secretariat for a drafting note, which would settle the interpretation in practice.
options.misconception: lets the party applying the rule also define it

questions.explanation: A standing rule that has been applied to membership cannot be reinterpreted by the party that applies it; that requires a decision by the assembly itself. Practical difficulty is a reason to seek a change, not a licence to change the rule unilaterally.
questions.hint: Ask who is entitled to change a rule they must apply.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: Characteristics of a global public good
questions.learningObjective: Judge whether a shared good is truly non-excludable
questions.stem: A global early-warning system issues alerts free to all countries, but a country can lose access if it fails to file its own sensor data. Which classification is best supported?

options.text: A private good, because access depends on each country's own payment of data.
options.misconception: reverses the condition, which concerns data not payment

options.text: A global public good with a partial exception, because non-contributors can be excluded from alerts.
A pure global public good, because the underlying science is freely available to everyone.
options.misconception: confuses free access to science with non-excludability of the service

options.text: A club good, because only countries that file data may participate in the system.
options.misconception: relabels a conditional public good as an exclusive club

questions.explanation: The alerts are non-rival, but the filing condition lets the provider withhold access from non-contributors, so non-excludability holds only in part. Free access to the underlying science does not remove the condition attached to the alert service.
questions.hint: Check whether anyone can be cut off from the benefit.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Evaluate a funding rule that leaves free-riding open
questions.stem: Seven member firms fund a shared standards library costing 210,000 a year. Six pay 30,000 each and one pays nothing, yet still queries the library. If the shortfall of 30,000 is spread evenly over the six paying firms, what extra does each pay?

options.text: 5,000, because the shortfall is shared by all seven firms including the non-payer.
options.misconception: spreads the shortfall over the free rider as well

options.text: 30,000, because each paying firm must absorb the whole non-payment.
options.misconception: adds the entire shortfall to every paying firm

options.text: 5,000, because 30,000 divided among the six paying firms is 5,000 each.
4,285, because the shortfall is divided by seven to keep the non-payer's slot fair.
options.misconception: divides the shortfall by seven rather than by the paying firms

questions.explanation: The unpaid share is 30,000 and six firms carry it, so each pays 5,000 more than before. Spreading the shortfall over seven firms would let the non-payer escape part of its obligation, which defeats the point of a cost rule.
questions.hint: Divide the shortfall by the firms that are actually paying.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Identify the step that turns a proposal into a binding commitment
questions.stem: In a standard treaty-making sequence, a provision becomes legally binding on a party only after which step?

options.text: After the working group circulates the first draft text to member states.
options.misconception: treats circulation of a draft as the source of legal obligation

options.text: After the drafting committee adopts the text unanimously by consensus.
options.misconception: treats committee consensus as the point of legal commitment

options.text: After the depositing state announces the opening of the signature period.
options.misconception: confuses the start of signatures with the creation of obligations

options.text: After the party deposits its instrument of ratification and the entry-into-force condition is met.

questions.explanation: Legal force on a party follows its own deposit of an instrument of ratification, once the entry-into-force condition is satisfied. Drafting, committee consensus, and the opening of signatures are preparatory steps that create no duty.
questions.hint: Ask what the party itself must deposit.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: Why states comply with rules they did not write
questions.learningObjective: Interpret compliance data with incentives attached
questions.stem: Jurisdiction A complied in 9 of 10 monitoring periods before a reporting obligation applied and in 10 of 10 afterwards; Jurisdiction B went from 4 of 10 to 10 of 10 over the same change. What does the comparison indicate?

options.text: Compliance was already high in A, so the change affected B far more in absolute terms.
A was fully compliant only because of the obligation, since it reached 10 of 10 after it applied.
options.misconception: ignores that A was already near full compliance beforehand

options.text: B resisted longer than A, which shows B's rules were more effective than A's.
options.misconception: reads a larger gain as evidence of a stronger legal regime

options.text: The data cannot distinguish incentives from voluntary change, since no baseline period is shown.
options.misconception: claims an absence of baseline data that the figures provide

questions.explanation: A was already close to full compliance before the obligation applied, so its change from nine to ten is smaller than B's jump from four to ten. That points to the obligation mattering most where compliance was initially weak.
questions.hint: Compare the size of each jurisdiction's change, not the final levels.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Explain the limits of treaty sovereignty constraints
questions.stem: A state has ratified an emissions protocol and a fisheries protocol that cover different fields. Explain what sovereignty the state retains after ratifying both.

answer.exemplar: The state remains sovereign in the sense that it still possesses the authority to govern, legislate, and act in every field not covered by the two protocols. Within the covered fields it has accepted specific limits on its own conduct, and it keeps the usual rights of a party, such as participation in the committees that interpret and apply the texts, the ability to seek amendments, and the right to withdraw under the terms the protocols set. What has changed is the room for unilateral discretion inside two defined areas, not the state's standing as an independent authority.

questions.explanation: Ratification constrains conduct in the covered fields while leaving the state sovereign elsewhere, with the usual participation and withdrawal rights preserved. Sovereignty survives as the capacity to govern, not as freedom from all limits.
questions.hint: Separate the two covered fields from everything else.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Compute the items still outstanding to meet a register target
questions.stem: A working group of 12 reviewers must produce 18 verified items each to meet a register target of 216 items, and exactly half of the items have been filed so far. How many items are still outstanding?
questions.explanation: Half of 216 is 108 items filed, leaving 216 minus 108, or 108 items outstanding. The per-reviewer quota of 18 confirms that the full target is 12 times 18, so the half-filed figure is exactly half of the requirement.
questions.hint: Take half of the target and subtract it from the whole.
